newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa Saldanha oil decision now due mid-year.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa Saldanha oil decision now due mid-year.

text.p: South Africa is now expected to make a final decision on whether to commercialise the Strategic Fuel Fund's (SFF) Saldanha oil storage terminal by mid-year, the state oil trader said on Tuesday.
SFF general manager Kobus van Zyl said that long-delayed environmental impact assessment work on commercialising the terminal should be completed by the end of March.

The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research would then draft a final report, which would be considered by a special review panel of experts. The panel would then make a recommendation to the government, which would make the final decision.
"We need the government's support because where the environment is involved you need the highest possible decision making level," Van Zyl said.
He admitted that the study had taken longer than expected because environmental impact assessments were no longer purely a scientific study.
"The whole community is involved in it and you need to consult fairly widely."
The study was started at the beginning of 1996 after SFF had announced that Iran was interested in storing some of its surplus oil stocks at the 45 million barrel facility.
There was widespread public concern that the increased tanker traffic would have adverse environmental effects on the sensitive wetlands around Saldanha.

Van Zyl said that two out of the 12 studies undertaken still had to be finalised. The study on the possible effect on ground and marine water, as well as soil, had been completed but was still subject to peer review. The cost-benefit analysis still had to be completed.
Van Zyl said that Iran was still interested in using the terminal at some future date and he was sure that other oil producers could be interested too, if the world oil market stabilised.
"I do not know how long the oil market will behave as it is behaving now. It depends on supply and demand but from what I read in the press, it is going to take some time," he said.

He said other oil producers had not been approached about using the storage facilities at Saldanha, but added: "For the same reason that Iran is interested, other large ones like the Saudis may be interested...I have not spoken to them about it but one must assume that something that will work for Iran may also work for other countries."
Progress in reducing South Africa's oil stockpile built up under apartheid era sanctions was ongoing, he added.
About 700,000 to one million barrels were being sold to South Africa's Natref refinery each month in a process that should be completed by October, Van Zyl said.
The government decided last year to reduce the stockpile to 36 million barrels from 48 million barrels.
